title: Python Day 01 — Data Types & Memory Management

lecture.New_PyDay01Audio01.mp3: Welcome to Day 01 of Python for Data Analysis! Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language known for its clean syntax and readability. Created by Guido van Rossum in 1991, Python emphasizes code simplicity, enabling developers and analysts to express complex logic in fewer lines of code than traditional languages like C++ or Java. Why Data Analysts Need Python? For data analyst, Python gives you five indispensable superpowers: first, loading and transforming massive datasets of 10 million rows or more where Excel freezes. second, building end-to-end automated ETL pipelines that run overnight without manual effort. third, executing advanced statistical modeling, grouping, and regex data cleaning with Pandas and NumPy. fourth, rendering interactive dashboards and charts with Seaborn and Plotly fifth, acting as your direct gateway into machine learning and modern generative AI.
lecture.New_PyDay01Audio02.mp3: Now, Let's examine the Analytics Tool Matrix: SQL versus Excel versus Python. SQL is your enterprise database workhorse, lightning-fast at filtering, joining, and aggregating billions of records directly inside the warehouse. Excel is your agile scratchpad for ad-hoc exploration, quick formulas, and executive summaries under 1 million rows. Python is your automation engine and analytical powerhouse, excelling at complex multi-step transformations, statistical algorithms, API integrations, and predictive modeling. The highest-paid modern data analysts don't pick just one; they extract with SQL, engineer and analyze with Python, and communicate insights with executive dashboards.
lecture.New_PyDay01Audio03.mp3: In Python, every value is an object living in your computer's memory, and every object has an identity: its memory address. The big question is whether that object can be changed after it is created. The answer splits Python's data types into two families: Mutable objects and Immutable objects. Mutable objects, such as lists, dictionaries, and sets, can be modified in-place without changing their memory address. Immutable objects, including integers, floats, strings, and tuples, can never be changed once created. Any modification generates a brand new object at a new memory address. Watch out for the dangerous Pitfall: writing clean data equals raw data does not create a copy, it creates an alias pointing to the exact same memory! Modifying clean data will silently corrupt your raw source. Always use dot copy to safeguard your analytical pipelines.
lecture.New_PyDay01Audio04.mp3: Here is the Master Data Types Reference matrix for data analysts. The table is organised by category, exactly as it appears on screen. Starting with Numeric types: Integer, written int, is an arbitrary-precision whole number that never overflows. Float is an IEEE-754 double-precision decimal, ideal for currency and averages. Complex stores real and imaginary parts for scientific work. Moving to Text: String, written str, is an immutable Unicode sequence and the workhorse for categorical columns. Boolean, written bool, is simply True or False, and it controls every analytical branch you write. The Sequence family holds ordered collections: List is mutable and perfect for a column of rows, Tuple is immutable and protects fixed records, and Range generates lazy integer sequences for memory-efficient iteration. Mapping means Dictionary, written dict, which stores key-value pairs and gives you lightning-fast O of 1 lookups using a hash table. Set types eliminate duplicates automatically and power fast union and intersection operations; Frozen Set is the immutable, hashable version safe to use as a dictionary key. And finally, NoneType is the singleton that represents missing or null data, just like SQL NULL.
lecture.New_PyDay01Audio05.mp3: Let's trace how Python manages memory under the hood through our runtime execution pipeline. When you run Python code, Python first allocates object values inside heap memory. Variables are not boxes that hold values; they are lightweight pointers or name tags bound to memory addresses. When two variables are assigned the same value, they point to the exact same object in RAM. Reassigning a variable does not overwrite the old data; it simply repoints the tag to a new memory location. To test whether two variables share the exact same memory address, use the is keyword, which checks object identity via memory IDs, compared to double equals, which checks value equality. Python automatically frees unused memory using reference counting and a cyclic garbage collector.

questions.New_PyDay01Question01.mp3: Welcome to your first Python exercise! Use Python's built-in print function to output the greeting: Hello, Python for Data Analysis! to the console.
questions.New_PyDay01Question01sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We call the print function and pass the string Hello, Python for Data Analysis inside quotation marks. When run, Python displays this text in the terminal.
questions.New_PyDay01Question02.mp3: Let's perform calculations with print! The print function can directly calculate math expressions. Use print to compute and display the sum of 150 plus 250.
questions.New_PyDay01Question02sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We write print opening parenthesis, 150 plus 250, closing parenthesis. Python calculates the arithmetic expression first and outputs 400.
questions.New_PyDay01Question03.mp3: Printing multiple values! You can print multiple items in a single line separated by commas. Use print to output the label 'Total Records:' followed by the number 500.
questions.New_PyDay01Question03sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We pass two arguments into print separated by a comma: the string label 'Total Records:' and the number 500. Python formats them separated by a space.
questions.New_PyDay01Question04.mp3: Creating an integer variable! Integers store whole numbers without decimals. Create a variable named employee count set to 150, and print it with the label 'Employee Count:'.
questions.New_PyDay01Question04sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We assign employee count equals 150, then call print passing the label and variable. Python looks up the variable's integer pointer and displays 150.
questions.New_PyDay01Question05.mp3: Creating a float variable! Floats store decimal numbers. Create a float variable named average salary set to 75450.50, and print it with the label 'Average Salary:'.
questions.New_PyDay01Question05sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We assign average salary equals 75450.50, then print it with its label. Python stores decimal numbers as 64-bit IEEE double-precision floats.
questions.New_PyDay01Question06.mp3: Creating a string variable! Strings store text enclosed in quotation marks. Create a string variable named company name set to 'Manodemy', and print it with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question06sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We assign company name equals 'Manodemy' in quotes, then print it with its label. Python creates an immutable string object in memory.
questions.New_PyDay01Question07.mp3: Creating a boolean variable! Booleans represent truth values and must be capitalized: True or False. Create a variable named is full time set to True, and print it with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question07sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We write is full time equals True with a capital T, and print it. Python booleans are singletons used for conditional logic.
questions.New_PyDay01Question08.mp3: Creating a list! Lists are ordered, mutable sequences defined inside square brackets. Create a list named sales figures containing 1200, 1450, and 1800, and print it with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question08sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We write sales figures equals opening bracket, 1200, 1450, 1800, closing bracket. Lists allow you to add, remove, and modify elements in place. Then we print the list with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question09.mp3: Creating a tuple! Tuples are ordered, immutable sequences defined in parentheses. Create a tuple named server location with 'Mumbai', 19.07, and 72.87, and print it with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question09sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We define server location equals parentheses containing 'Mumbai', 19.07, and 72.87. Tuples protect coordinates and dimensions from accidental modification. Then we print the tuple with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question10.mp3: Creating a dictionary! Dictionaries store key-value pairs in curly braces. Create a dictionary named customer profile with name 'Aarav' and orders 5, and print it with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question10sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We assign customer profile equals curly braces, key 'name' colon 'Aarav', comma, key 'orders' colon 5. Dictionaries provide fast O of 1 lookups by key. Then we print the dictionary with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question11.mp3: Creating a set! Sets store unique elements inside curly braces. Create a set named unique tags containing 'python', 'sql', and 'analytics', and print it with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question11sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We assign unique tags equals curly braces containing 'python', 'sql', and 'analytics'. Sets automatically discard duplicate entries. Then we print the set with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question12.mp3: The NoneType singleton! In Python, None represents missing or null data. Create a variable named bonus amount set to None with a capital N, and print it with its label.
questions.New_PyDay01Question12sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We write bonus amount equals None with a capital N. Then we print it with its label. None is Python's standard singleton for representing the absence of a value.
questions.New_PyDay01Question13.mp3: Composite fraud detection! Group transaction amounts across multi-dimensional keys user id, device, and ip into a dictionary called fraud map, using a tuple-keyed defaultdict of float.
questions.New_PyDay01Question13sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We import defaultdict from collections. Then we build a list called transactions holding four sample records. The first record has user id U zero one, device mobile, ip address ten dot zero dot zero dot one, and amount one twenty point five zero. The second record repeats user U zero one and mobile, with amount three forty. The third record is user U zero two on desktop, ip one nine two dot one six eight dot one dot five, amount eighty five point seven five. The fourth record is user U zero one, mobile, ip ten dot zero dot zero dot two, amount five hundred. Now we create an empty fraud map using defaultdict of float, so a missing key defaults to zero point zero. We loop through each transaction. We build a tuple key from user id, device, and ip. Then we add the transaction amount into fraud map at that key. Finally we print the fraud map, converted to a regular dictionary, which shows the total amount per unique combination.
questions.New_PyDay01Question14.mp3: Recursive dict flattener! Write a recursive function called flatten dict that takes a nested dictionary and a parent key, and returns a flat dictionary with dot-separated keys, coalescing any None values to the string N/A.
questions.New_PyDay01Question14sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We build a dictionary called nested. It has a key user, whose value is another dictionary with key name, set to Aarav, and key address, which holds key city set to Mumbai and key pin set to None. It also has key score, set to ninety five. Then we define a function called flatten dict that takes a dictionary d and a parent key, and creates an empty dictionary called items. We loop over each key value pair in d using the items method. We build a new key: if parent key exists, we combine parent key, a dot, and the current key using an f string; otherwise the new key is just k. If the value is a dictionary, we check with isinstance, and recursively call flatten dict with the value and the new key, then update items. Otherwise, we set items at the new key to the value, or to the string N/A if the value is None. We return items. Finally we call flatten dict on nested, store the result in flat, and print flat.
questions.New_PyDay01Question15.mp3: Dynamic list allocator tracking! Create an empty list called lst and a list called jump sizes. Loop through the integers zero to twenty using range of twenty one, appending each index to lst. Every time the size of lst jumps, append the index and the new size as a tuple to jump sizes. Finally print jump sizes.
questions.New_PyDay01Question15sol.mp3: Here is the solution. We import sys. Then we create an empty list called lst. We also create an empty list called jump sizes. We measure the size of lst using sys dot getsizeof, and store that value in prev size. We loop from 0 to 20 using range of 21. Inside the loop, we append i to lst. Then we measure the size of lst again with getsizeof, and store it in cur size. If cur size is greater than prev size, we append the tuple of i and cur size to jump sizes, and we update prev size to cur size. Finally we print jump sizes, and that is our complete answer.
